newsitem.title: UK: Diana denies marriage plans as Camilla talk swirls.
newsitem.headline: Diana denies marriage plans as Camilla talk swirls.

text.p: Princess Diana denied on Sunday that she had become engaged to a Pakistani heart surgeon, while speculation surfaced that Prince Charles might marry his mistress, Camilla Parker Bowles, in a "non-royal" wedding.
Diana's office tersely dismissed a front-page report in the Sunday Mirror that she had become unofficially engaged to Hasnat Khan, 38, a leading London-based heart surgeon.
"The Princess of Wales has not become engaged to Dr Hasnat Khan, officially or unofficially," a spokesman said.
"Continuing speculation of this nature is untrue, and more importantly, disruptive to the hospitals that Dr Khan works in," he added.
The paper said the love-struck princess, 36, who divorced Charles last year, flew to Pakistan last month in an attempt to persuade Khan's mother to let the couple marry.
The charm offensive worked, the Sunday Mirror said.
"Princess Diana and Hasnat Khan are, to all intents and purposes, engaged to be married," it reported.

Another newspaper, The Sunday Times, said friends of heir-to-the-throne Charles and his long-time flame Camilla were preparing the ground for a non-royal "morganatic" marriage so they could live a "more honest and contented life together".

It said a growing group of influential figures believed a morganatic marriage, which would allow Charles to remarry without conferring royal status on Camilla, would give him emotional stability and guarantee a successful reign.
"Such a marriage would be unprecedented in British history and ministers believe it is unlikely to happen until the dust settles on Prince Charles's divorce from Diana..." The Sunday Times said.
"Some, however, believe he is likely to marry Parker Bowles before the next general election, which must be held by 2002," it added.

The idea behind a morganatic marriage, which would require legislation to amend a 1772 act of parliament, would be to overcome popular hostility to a Charles-Camilla wedding. There are no constitutional hurdles to his remarrying.
But the Sunday Times quoted a Conservative adviser to Queen Elizabeth as saying: "It would be a hell of a gamble. I couldn't guarantee what would happen to the monarchy if you went down that road."
